questions.prompt: Change into indirect speech: He said, "I was reading a book."
options: He said that he was reading a book.
He said that he has been reading a book.
He said that he had been reading a book.
He said that he is reading a book.
questions.explanation: Past continuous in direct speech → past perfect continuous in indirect speech.
questions.trick: Past continuous → past perfect continuous.

questions.prompt: Change into indirect speech: She said, "I shall be late."
options: She said that she shall be late.
She said that she will be late.
She said that she was being late.
She said that she would be late.
questions.explanation: When the reported speaker becomes 'she', 'shall' becomes 'would'.

questions.prompt: Change into indirect speech: He said to me, "Why are you angry?"
options: He asked me why was I angry.
He asked me why I was angry.
He asked me why I am angry.
He asked me that why I was angry.
questions.explanation: Wh-question → asked + wh-word + subject + verb; are → was; no 'that'.

questions.prompt: Change into indirect speech: The beggar said to me, "Please give me some food."
options: The beggar ordered me to give him some food.
The beggar requested me to give him some food.
The beggar requested me to give me some food.
The beggar told me that give him some food.
questions.explanation: 'Please' signals a request → 'requested + object + to-infinitive'; me (the beggar) → him.
questions.trick: please/kindly → requested.

questions.prompt: Change into indirect speech: Father said, "Let us go to the beach."
options: Father proposed that they should go to the beach.
Father ordered that they go to the beach.
Father said let us go to the beach.
Father proposed that let us go to the beach.
questions.explanation: 'Let us' (a suggestion) is reported with 'proposed/suggested that … should'.

questions.prompt: Change into indirect speech: She said to him, "Do you like coffee?"
options: She asked him if he likes coffee.
She asked him did he like coffee.
She asked him if you liked coffee.
She asked him if he liked coffee.
questions.explanation: do you like → if he liked (past, statement order).

questions.prompt: Change into direct speech: "The teacher asked the boy whether he had done his homework."
options: The teacher said to the boy, "Had you done your homework?"
The teacher said to the boy, "Did you done your homework?"
The teacher said to the boy, "Have you done your homework?"
The teacher said to the boy, "Have I done my homework?"
questions.explanation: Reverse the shift: had done → have done; he (the boy, the listener) → you; 'whether' → a direct question.

questions.prompt: Change into indirect speech: The doctor said to the patient, "Take this medicine twice a day."
options: The doctor advised the patient to take this medicine twice a day.
The doctor advised the patient to take that medicine twice a day.
The doctor said the patient take that medicine twice a day.
The doctor advised the patient that take that medicine twice a day.
questions.explanation: Advice is reported with 'advised + object + to-infinitive', and 'this' changes to 'that'.

questions.prompt: Change into indirect speech: "Who are you?" the watchman asked the boy.
options: The watchman asked the boy who was he.
The watchman asked the boy who he is.
The watchman asked the boy who he was.
The watchman asked the boy who are you.
questions.explanation: Wh-question → statement order (who he was); are → was; you → he.

questions.prompt: Change into positive degree: "Kavitha is one of the best singers in our school."
options: No other singer in our school is as good as Kavitha.
Kavitha is as good as other singers in our school.
Some singers in our school are better than Kavitha.
Very few singers in our school are as good as Kavitha.
questions.explanation: 'One of the + superlative' means only a few others match it → 'Very few … are as … as …'.
questions.trick: 'One of the …est' → Positive: Very few … as … as; Comparative: …er than most other …

questions.prompt: Change into superlative degree: "No other boy in the class is as tall as Ravi."
options: Ravi is the tallest boy in the class.
Ravi is taller than any boy in the class.
Ravi is very tall in the class.
Ravi is as tall as the other boys in the class.
questions.explanation: 'No other … as … as X' means X is the -est.
questions.trick: No other … as … as X → X is the …est.

questions.prompt: Change into positive degree: "Gold is more precious than silver."
options: Gold is as precious as silver.
Silver is as precious as gold.
Silver is not more precious than gold.
Silver is not as precious as gold.
questions.explanation: A is more … than B → B is not as/so … as A.
questions.trick: A is …er than B → B is not so/as … as A.

questions.prompt: Change into comparative degree: "Sachin is the best batsman in our club."
options: Sachin is better than all batsman in our club.
Sachin is more better than any batsman in our club.
Sachin is better than any other batsman in our club.
Sachin is good than any other batsman in our club.
questions.explanation: Superlative 'the best' → comparative 'better than any other' (include 'other', since Sachin is himself in the club).

questions.prompt: Change into comparative degree: "Few cities in India are as old as Madurai."
options: Madurai is older than most other cities in India.
Madurai is older than any other city in India.
Madurai is the oldest city in India.
Madurai is as old as other cities in India.
questions.explanation: 'Few … as old as' means it is among the oldest, not the single oldest → 'older than most other'.

questions.prompt: The comparative degree of 'little' (amount) is:
questions.explanation: little – less – least (irregular comparison).

questions.prompt: The superlative degree of 'far' (distance) is:
questions.explanation: far – farther – farthest (furthest is also used); 'farest' and 'farer' do not exist.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: "Raju is ___ than his sister by three years."
questions.explanation: 'Elder' is not followed by 'than'; with 'than' we use 'older'.
questions.trick: elder/eldest → only for family, never with 'than'.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: "Have you read the ___ issue of this magazine? It came out only today."
questions.explanation: 'Latest' means most recent; 'last' means final in a series.
questions.trick: latest = newest; last = final.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: "Which is the ___ of the two books?"
questions.explanation: When only two are compared, the comparative is used.
questions.trick: Of the two → comparative; of three or more → superlative.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: "Meena is the ___ of the three sisters."
questions.explanation: With three or more, use the superlative: prettiest.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: "Arun is ___ intelligent than his brother."
questions.explanation: Long adjectives form the comparative with 'more … than'.

questions.prompt: Identify the degree of comparison: "No other river in India is as long as the Ganga."
questions.explanation: 'As long as' uses the base (positive) form of the adjective.
questions.trick: as … as / so … as → positive degree.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: "This lane is ___ than the main road."
questions.explanation: Comparing two things with 'than' requires the comparative: narrower.

questions.prompt: Spot the part of the sentence that has an error: "He is / more cleverer / than / his brother."
questions.explanation: A double comparative is wrong: use 'cleverer' or 'more clever', not 'more cleverer'.
questions.trick: Never combine more/most with -er/-est.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: "Iron is ___ useful than any other metal."
questions.explanation: 'Than any other' needs the comparative degree: more useful.

questions.prompt: Change into superlative degree: "Very few students are as hardworking as Priya."
options: Priya is one of the most hardworking students.
Priya is the most hardworking student.
Priya is more hardworking than any other student.
Priya is as hardworking as other students.
questions.explanation: 'Very few … as … as' corresponds to 'one of the most …' (not the single best).

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: "Of all the planets in the solar system, Jupiter is ___."
questions.explanation: Jupiter is the biggest planet; 'of all' requires the superlative with 'the'.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
options: Your suggestion is preferable than mine.
Your suggestion is more preferable than mine.
Your suggestion is most preferable to mine.
Your suggestion is preferable to mine.
questions.explanation: 'Preferable' already has a comparative meaning and takes 'to'; 'more preferable' is wrong.
questions.trick: prefer / preferable → TO, never 'than' or 'more'.

questions.prompt: The comparative degree of 'many' is:
questions.explanation: many – more – most.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: "This is the ___ building in our city."
questions.explanation: Comparing one with all others → superlative: the tallest.

questions.prompt: Change into comparative degree: "Ravi is not as strong as Raman."
options: Raman is as strong as Ravi.
questions.explanation: B is not as … as A → A is …er than B.

questions.prompt: Which adjective is normally NOT used in the comparative or superlative degree?
questions.explanation: 'Unique' means 'the only one of its kind', so it cannot be more or less unique.
questions.trick: Absolute adjectives — unique, perfect, complete, round, square — are not compared.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: "The ___ you practise, the more confident you become."
questions.explanation: The parallel comparative 'the more …, the more …' uses the comparative in both parts.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: "She carefully avoided ___ him at the wedding."
questions.explanation: 'Avoid' is followed by a gerund, not an infinitive.
questions.trick: Gerund-only verbs: avoid, enjoy, finish, mind, deny, practise, consider, can't help. Infinitive-only: want, decide, hope, refuse, agree, promise.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: "I want ___ a doctor when I grow up."
questions.explanation: 'Want' is followed by a to-infinitive.
questions.trick: Gerund-only verbs: avoid, enjoy, finish, mind, deny, practise, consider, can't help. Infinitive-only: want, decide, hope, refuse, agree, promise.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: "Would you mind ___ the window?"
questions.explanation: 'Mind' is followed by a gerund.
questions.trick: Gerund-only verbs: avoid, enjoy, finish, mind, deny, practise, consider, can't help. Infinitive-only: want, decide, hope, refuse, agree, promise.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: "After much thought, he decided ___ the job offer."
questions.explanation: 'Decide' is followed by a to-infinitive.
questions.trick: Gerund-only verbs: avoid, enjoy, finish, mind, deny, practise, consider, can't help. Infinitive-only: want, decide, hope, refuse, agree, promise.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: "She is interested in ___ portraits."
questions.explanation: A verb after a preposition (in) takes the -ing (gerund) form.
questions.trick: After a preposition (in, of, at, about, without, to in 'look forward to') use the -ing form.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: "I look forward to ___ you at the reunion."
questions.explanation: In 'look forward to', 'to' is a preposition, so it is followed by a gerund.
questions.trick: 'to' as a PREPOSITION → -ing: look forward to, be used to, object to, with a view to.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: "My grandfather is used to ___ up at five every morning."
questions.explanation: 'Be used to' (be accustomed to) takes a gerund; compare 'He used to get up early' (past habit).
questions.trick: be used to + -ing = accustomed to; used to + base verb = past habit.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: "The teacher made him ___ the work again."
questions.explanation: 'Make + object' is followed by a bare infinitive (without 'to') in the active voice.
questions.trick: make / let / had better / would rather + object + BARE infinitive (no 'to').

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: "Let me ___ you carry that bag."
questions.explanation: 'Let + object' takes a bare infinitive.
questions.trick: make / let / had better / would rather + object + BARE infinitive (no 'to').

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: "You had better ___ a doctor about that cough."
questions.explanation: 'Had better' is followed by a bare infinitive.
questions.trick: make / let / had better / would rather + object + BARE infinitive (no 'to').

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: "I would rather ___ at home than go out in this rain."
questions.explanation: 'Would rather' is followed by a bare infinitive.
questions.trick: make / let / had better / would rather + object + BARE infinitive (no 'to').

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: "The ___ child was rescued by the fireman."
questions.explanation: The child felt fear, so the past participle 'frightened' (passive feeling) is used as an adjective.
questions.trick: -ing adjective = causes the feeling (a boring film); -ed adjective = has the feeling (a bored audience).

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: "The final match was so ___ that nobody left their seats."
questions.explanation: The match caused excitement, so the -ing participle adjective is used.
questions.trick: -ing adjective = causes the feeling; -ed adjective = has the feeling.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: "The students were ___ with their examination results."
questions.explanation: The students felt the disappointment, so the past participle form is used.
questions.trick: -ing adjective = causes the feeling; -ed adjective = has the feeling.

questions.prompt: Identify the infinitive in the sentence: "She came here to meet the principal."
questions.explanation: An infinitive is 'to' + base form of a verb: to meet.

questions.prompt: Identify the gerund in the sentence: "Smoking is injurious to health."
questions.explanation: 'Smoking' is a verb + -ing used as a noun (the subject of the sentence), so it is a gerund.

questions.prompt: In "I saw a man carrying a heavy box," the word 'carrying' is a:
questions.explanation: 'Carrying' describes the man (acts like an adjective), so it is a present participle, not a gerund.
questions.trick: -ing as a noun → gerund; -ing describing a noun → participle.

questions.prompt: In "He is fond of reading detective stories," the word 'reading' is a:
questions.explanation: 'Reading' is the object of the preposition 'of' — it works as a noun, so it is a gerund.

questions.prompt: In "The broken chair was repaired," the word 'broken' is a:
questions.explanation: 'Broken' (third form of 'break') describes the chair — a past participle used as an adjective.

questions.prompt: In "I have a lot of work to do," the infinitive 'to do' functions as a/an:
questions.explanation: 'To do' tells which work — it qualifies the noun 'work', so it is used as an adjective.

questions.prompt: In "He went to the market to buy vegetables," the infinitive 'to buy' expresses:
questions.explanation: 'To buy vegetables' tells why he went — the infinitive of purpose.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: "Don't forget ___ off the lights before you leave."
questions.explanation: 'Forget + to-infinitive' refers to a duty still to be done; 'forget + -ing' refers to a past memory.
questions.trick: remember/forget + to = something still to do; + -ing = something already done.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: "The honest officer refused ___ the bribe."
questions.explanation: 'Refuse' is followed by a to-infinitive.
questions.trick: Gerund-only verbs: avoid, enjoy, finish, mind, deny, practise, consider, can't help. Infinitive-only: want, decide, hope, refuse, agree, promise.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: "It is no use ___ over spilt milk."
questions.explanation: The expression 'It is no use' is followed by a gerund.
questions.trick: it's no use / it's worth / can't help / can't stand → -ing.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: "I couldn't help ___ at his funny jokes."
questions.explanation: 'Can't/couldn't help' (cannot avoid) is followed by a gerund.
questions.trick: it's no use / it's worth / can't help / can't stand → -ing.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: "The thief was seen ___ the building through the back door."
questions.explanation: In the active, 'see' takes a bare infinitive (saw him enter), but in the passive 'to' returns: was seen to enter.
questions.trick: Bare infinitive after make/see/hear in the active → to-infinitive in the passive.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: "He was made ___ the fine for late payment."
questions.explanation: Active 'They made him pay' becomes passive 'He was made to pay' — 'to' is added.
questions.trick: Bare infinitive after make/see/hear in the active → to-infinitive in the passive.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: "This novel is really worth ___."
questions.explanation: 'Worth' is followed by a gerund (active form, passive meaning).
questions.trick: it's no use / it's worth / can't help → -ing.

questions.prompt: Which of these verbs is followed by a to-infinitive and NOT by a gerund?
questions.explanation: We say 'I hope to win', never 'hope winning'; enjoy, avoid and finish take gerunds.
questions.trick: Gerund-only verbs: avoid, enjoy, finish, mind, deny, practise, consider, can't help. Infinitive-only: want, decide, hope, refuse, agree, promise.

questions.prompt: In "Having finished his work, he went home," the words 'Having finished' form a:
questions.explanation: Having + past participle = perfect participle; it shows an action completed before another.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: "He strongly objected to ___ treated like a child."
questions.explanation: In 'object to', 'to' is a preposition, so it is followed by a gerund: being treated.
questions.trick: After a preposition (in, of, at, about, without, to in 'look forward to') use the -ing form.

questions.prompt: The past participle of 'swim' is:
questions.explanation: swim – swam – swum.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: "Feeling unwell, he ___ down on the bed for an hour."
questions.explanation: 'Lie' (to rest) has the forms lie – lay – lain; 'laid' belongs to 'lay' (to put), and 'lied' means told a lie.
questions.trick: lie (rest): lie-lay-lain; lay (put): lay-laid-laid; lie (untruth): lie-lied-lied.

questions.prompt: Identify the sentence pattern: "Birds fly."
questions.explanation: Only a subject (Birds) and an intransitive verb (fly).
questions.trick: Find the verb first, then ask 'who/what?' before it (S), 'whom/what?' after it (O); C completes S or O; A tells when/where/how.

questions.prompt: Identify the sentence pattern: "The boy kicked the ball."
questions.explanation: The boy (S) kicked (V) the ball (O).
questions.trick: Find the verb first, then ask 'who/what?' before it (S), 'whom/what?' after it (O); C completes S or O; A tells when/where/how.

questions.prompt: Identify the sentence pattern: "My father is a teacher."
questions.explanation: 'A teacher' completes the meaning of the subject after the linking verb 'is', so it is a subject complement.
questions.trick: After be/become/seem/look/appear/grow/turn → Complement, not Object.

questions.prompt: Identify the sentence pattern: "Grandmother is in the garden."
questions.explanation: 'In the garden' tells where — it is an adverbial, not a complement.

questions.prompt: Identify the sentence pattern: "Mother gave me a book."
questions.explanation: me = indirect object (to whom), a book = direct object (what).
questions.trick: Two objects not equal to each other → IO + DO; if the second describes the first → O + C.

questions.prompt: Identify the sentence pattern: "They elected him president."
questions.explanation: 'President' describes 'him' (him = president), so it is an object complement.
questions.trick: Two objects not equal to each other → IO + DO; if the second describes the first → O + C.

questions.prompt: Identify the sentence pattern: "He kept the money in the safe."
questions.explanation: He (S) kept (V) the money (O) in the safe (A — place).
questions.trick: Find the verb first, then ask 'who/what?' before it (S), 'whom/what?' after it (O); C completes S or O; A tells when/where/how.

questions.prompt: Identify the sentence pattern: "Every morning, Raju walks."
questions.explanation: 'Every morning' (A) comes first; Raju (S) walks (V, intransitive).

questions.prompt: Identify the sentence pattern: "The children are playing in the park."
questions.explanation: 'Are playing' is the verb and 'in the park' is an adverbial of place; there is no object.

questions.prompt: Identify the sentence pattern: "The teacher made the lesson interesting."
questions.explanation: 'Interesting' describes the object 'the lesson' → object complement.

questions.prompt: Identify the sentence pattern: "We reached the station at six."
questions.explanation: 'Reach' is transitive — 'the station' is its object; 'at six' is an adverbial of time.

questions.prompt: Identify the sentence pattern: "My brother became an engineer."
questions.explanation: 'Became' is a linking verb, so 'an engineer' is a subject complement.
questions.trick: After be/become/seem/look/appear/grow/turn → Complement, not Object.

questions.prompt: Identify the sentence pattern: "The milk turned sour."
questions.explanation: 'Turned' is a linking verb here; 'sour' describes the subject → complement.

questions.prompt: Identify the sentence pattern: "She sent her friend a birthday card."
questions.explanation: her friend = indirect object; a birthday card = direct object.

questions.prompt: Identify the sentence pattern: "In the evening, we watched a film."
questions.explanation: In the evening (A), we (S) watched (V) a film (O).

questions.prompt: Identify the sentence pattern: "The old man looks tired."
questions.explanation: 'Looks' is a linking verb; 'tired' describes the subject.

questions.prompt: Identify the sentence pattern: "Ram placed the vase on the table carefully."
questions.explanation: Ram (S) placed (V) the vase (O) on the table (A — place) carefully (A — manner).

questions.prompt: Identify the indirect object: "She bought her son a bicycle."
questions.explanation: The indirect object answers 'for whom/to whom' — her son; 'a bicycle' is the direct object.

questions.prompt: Identify the complement: "The villagers appointed him their leader."
questions.explanation: 'Their leader' describes the object 'him' (him = their leader) — object complement.

questions.prompt: In "Sita sings sweetly," the word 'sweetly' is the:
questions.explanation: 'Sweetly' tells how she sings — an adverbial.

questions.prompt: Which element must be present in every sentence pattern?
questions.explanation: Every pattern (SV, SVO, SVC, SVA …) contains a verb; objects, complements and adverbials are optional.

questions.prompt: Pick the sentence whose pattern is Subject + Verb + Object (SVO).
questions.explanation: 'The flute' is the object of 'plays'. The others are SVC, SVA and SV.

questions.prompt: In which sentence is the word after the verb a subject complement (pattern SVC)?
options: The cook tasted the soup in the kitchen.
questions.explanation: 'Tastes' is a linking verb and 'delicious' describes the soup. The others are SVO, SVOA and SVIODO.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence that has an object followed by an adverbial of place (SVOA).
options: She put the keys in her bag.
questions.explanation: She (S) put (V) the keys (O) in her bag (A). The others are SVC, SVOC and SV.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a NON-finite verb form?
questions.explanation: Non-finite forms (infinitive, gerund, participle) do not change with the subject or tense.
questions.trick: Finite verbs change with person/number/tense; non-finites (to-V, V-ing, V3) do not.

questions.prompt: Identify the finite verb in: "Seeing the police, the thief ran away."
questions.explanation: 'Ran' shows tense and has a subject (the thief); 'Seeing' is a participle (non-finite).

questions.prompt: Match the non-finite verbs. (a) To err is human. (b) I saw him running. (c) Swimming is good exercise. (d) The stolen car was found. — 1. Gerund 2. Infinitive 3. Present participle 4. Past participle
questions.explanation: To err = infinitive; running (describing him) = present participle; Swimming (subject) = gerund; stolen = past participle.

questions.prompt: In "Walking along the beach, I found a shell," the words 'Walking along the beach' form a:
questions.explanation: It describes the subject 'I' and has no finite verb, so it is a participial phrase.

questions.prompt: In "His ambition is to become a pilot," the infinitive phrase 'to become a pilot' functions as the:
questions.explanation: It follows the linking verb 'is' and tells what his ambition is — a complement.

questions.prompt: Which sentence contains a dangling (misrelated) participle?
options: Running to the bus stop, I dropped my bag.
While I was running to the bus stop, my bag fell open.
Running to the bus stop, my bag fell open.
My bag fell open as I ran to the bus stop.
questions.explanation: The participle 'Running' seems to refer to 'my bag', which cannot run.
questions.trick: The participle must refer to the subject that follows the comma.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: "___ by the sudden noise, the baby started crying."
questions.explanation: The baby was frightened (passive meaning), so the past participle opens the sentence.

questions.prompt: Transform without changing the meaning: "He is too weak to walk."
options: He is so weak that he can walk.
He is so weak that he cannot walk.
He is so weak to walk.
He is very weak that he cannot walk.
questions.explanation: 'Too … to' carries a negative idea, so it becomes 'so … that … cannot'.
questions.trick: too … to = so … that … cannot (meaning stays negative).

questions.prompt: Transform using 'too … to': "She is so poor that she cannot buy a car."
options: She is too poor not to buy a car.
She is very poor to buy a car.
She is so poor to buy a car.
She is too poor to buy a car.
questions.explanation: 'So … that … cannot' becomes 'too … to' — the 'not' disappears because 'too' already carries it.
questions.trick: too … to = so … that … cannot (meaning stays negative).

questions.prompt: Begin with 'No sooner': "As soon as he saw the police, he ran away."
options: No sooner he saw the police than he ran away.
No sooner did he see the police when he ran away.
No sooner had he see the police then he ran away.
No sooner did he see the police than he ran away.
questions.explanation: 'No sooner' takes inversion (did he see) and is followed by 'than'.
questions.trick: No sooner … THAN; Hardly / Scarcely … WHEN — and the auxiliary comes before the subject (inversion).

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: "Hardly had the bell rung ___ the students rushed out."
questions.explanation: 'Hardly' and 'Scarcely' are paired with 'when', not 'than'.
questions.trick: No sooner … THAN; Hardly / Scarcely … WHEN — and the auxiliary comes before the subject (inversion).

questions.prompt: Convert into a complex sentence: "He confessed his guilt."
options: He confessed and he was guilty.
He confessed that he was guilty.
questions.explanation: The noun phrase 'his guilt' is expanded into a noun clause 'that he was guilty'.

questions.prompt: Convert into a simple sentence: "He worked hard and passed the exam."
options: He worked hard and so passed the exam.
By working hard, he passed the exam.
Because he worked hard, he passed the exam.
He worked hard, he passed the exam.
questions.explanation: A simple sentence has only one finite verb; 'working' is a non-finite form. The second option is still compound and the third is complex.
questions.trick: Simple = ONE finite verb; turn the extra clause into a phrase (participle, infinitive, prepositional phrase).

questions.prompt: Convert into a simple sentence: "When the sun rose, the fog cleared."
options: When the sun rose, fog cleared.
The sun rose and the fog cleared.
The sun rose, so the fog cleared.
questions.explanation: The adverb clause 'When the sun rose' is reduced to the phrase 'At sunrise', leaving one finite verb.

questions.prompt: Convert into a compound sentence: "In spite of his poverty, he is honest."
options: Though he is poor, he is honest.
In spite of being poor, he is honest.
He is poor, but he is honest.
questions.explanation: A compound sentence joins two main clauses with a coordinating conjunction (but). 'Though …' makes it complex.
questions.trick: Compound: and, but, or, so, yet. Complex: though, because, if, when, who, that.

questions.prompt: Convert into a compound sentence: "If you do not work hard, you will fail."
options: Work hard and you will fail.
Unless you work hard, you will fail.
Without hard work, you will fail.
Work hard, or you will fail.
questions.explanation: 'If … not' becomes 'or' (otherwise) joining two main clauses. The 'unless' version is still complex and the 'without' version is simple.

questions.prompt: Rewrite using 'If': "Unless you study, you will fail."
options: If you study, you will fail.
If you do not study, you will fail.
If you will not study, you fail.
Unless you do not study, you will fail.
questions.explanation: 'Unless' means 'if … not'.
questions.trick: unless = if … not; never put 'not' after 'unless'.

questions.prompt: Change into a negative sentence without changing the meaning: "Only Ravi passed the test."
options: Ravi did not pass the test.
Not only Ravi passed the test.
None but Ravi passed the test.
questions.explanation: 'Only' + person → 'None but' + person.
questions.trick: only (person) → none but; only (thing) → nothing but.

questions.prompt: Change into a negative sentence without changing the meaning: "He is always punctual."
questions.explanation: always → never, with the opposite word (punctual → late).

questions.prompt: Change into a negative sentence without changing the meaning: "Everybody loves his mother."
options: Everybody does not love his mother.
There is nobody who does not love his mother.
questions.explanation: Two negatives (nobody … not) give the same positive meaning.

questions.prompt: Change into an assertive sentence: "Who does not love his country?"
options: Everyone does not love his country.
questions.explanation: A rhetorical negative question becomes a positive statement.
questions.trick: Rhetorical question → statement of the OPPOSITE polarity (Who does not …? = Everyone …).

questions.prompt: Change into an assertive sentence: "Can anyone bear such an insult?"
options: Anyone can bear such an insult.
No one can bear such an insult.
Everyone can bear such an insult.
Someone cannot bear such an insult.
questions.explanation: A rhetorical positive question becomes a negative statement.
questions.trick: Rhetorical question → statement of the OPPOSITE polarity (Who does not …? = Everyone …).

questions.prompt: Change into an interrogative sentence: "Nobody can trust a liar."
options: Does anybody not trust a liar?
questions.explanation: A negative statement becomes a positive rhetorical question: Nobody can … → Who can …?
questions.trick: Rhetorical question → statement of the OPPOSITE polarity (Who does not …? = Everyone …).

questions.prompt: Change into an assertive sentence: "How foolish I have been!"
questions.explanation: In an exclamation, 'How + adjective' becomes 'very + adjective' in a statement.

questions.prompt: Change into an exclamatory sentence: "It is a very lovely morning."
options: What a lovely morning is it!
What a lovely morning it is!
What lovely a morning it is!
questions.explanation: 'very + adjective + noun' becomes 'What a + adjective + noun + subject + verb!' (statement word order).

questions.prompt: Identify the kind of sentence: "Do not waste your time."
questions.explanation: It gives a command/advice with an understood subject 'you'.

questions.prompt: Identify the kind of sentence: "Although he was ill, he attended the class."
questions.explanation: It has one main clause and one subordinate clause (introduced by 'Although').

questions.prompt: Identify the kind of sentence: "The sun rose and the birds began to sing."
questions.explanation: Two independent clauses joined by the coordinating conjunction 'and'.

questions.prompt: Identify the kind of sentence: "Despite the heavy rain, the match continued."
questions.explanation: There is only one finite verb (continued); 'Despite the heavy rain' is a phrase.

questions.prompt: Combine using 'not only … but also': "He is a poet. He is also a painter."
options: He is either a poet or a painter.
He is neither a poet nor a painter.
He is not only a poet but also a painter.
He is a poet but not a painter.
questions.explanation: 'Not only … but also' adds the second fact to the first.

questions.prompt: Combine using a relative pronoun: "This is the boy. He won the prize."
options: This is the boy which won the prize.
This is the boy whom won the prize.
This is the boy whose won the prize.
This is the boy who won the prize.
questions.explanation: 'Who' is the subject relative pronoun for persons.
questions.trick: who (person, subject), whom (person, object), whose (possession), which (things).

questions.prompt: Combine the sentences: "He was tired. He continued working."
options: Though he was tired, he continued working.
Because he was tired, he continued working.
He was tired, so he continued working.
If he was tired, he continued working.
questions.explanation: The two ideas contrast, so a concession conjunction (though/although) is needed.

questions.prompt: Combine the sentences: "The rain stopped. We went out."
options: Unless the rain stopped, we went out.
When the rain stopped, we went out.
Though the rain stopped, we went out.
Until the rain stopped, we went out.
questions.explanation: The second action follows the first in time, so 'When' fits.

questions.prompt: Combine using an infinitive: "He wants to pass the examination. So he works hard."
options: He works hard to pass the examination.
He works hard passing the examination.
He works hard for pass the examination.
He wants hard work to pass the examination.
questions.explanation: An infinitive of purpose (to pass) joins the two ideas in one simple sentence.

questions.prompt: Combine using a participle: "He opened the door. He went out."
options: Opened the door, he went out.
To open the door, he went out.
Opening the door, he went out.
He opening the door went out.
questions.explanation: The first action becomes a present participle phrase whose subject is the same 'he'.

questions.prompt: Combine using 'either … or': "You must apologise. Otherwise you will be punished."
options: Neither you must apologise nor you will be punished.
Either you must apologise or you will be punished.
Both you must apologise and you will be punished.
You must apologise but you will be punished.
questions.explanation: 'Either … or' presents two alternatives.

questions.prompt: Rewrite without changing the meaning: "He is cleverer than his brother."
options: He is not cleverer than his brother.
His brother is cleverer than he is.
He is not as clever as his brother.
His brother is not so clever as he is.
questions.explanation: A is …er than B → B is not so/as … as A.

questions.prompt: Convert into a statement: "Isn't it a beautiful day?"
options: It is not a beautiful day.
questions.explanation: A negative question expecting 'yes' becomes a positive statement.
questions.trick: Rhetorical question → statement of the OPPOSITE polarity (Who does not …? = Everyone …).

questions.prompt: Rewrite using 'so … that': "The tea was too hot to drink."
options: The tea was so hot that it could be drunk.
The tea was so hot to drink.
The tea was very hot that it could not be drunk.
The tea was so hot that it could not be drunk.
questions.explanation: 'Too … to' → 'so … that … could not' (past tense kept).
questions.trick: too … to = so … that … cannot (meaning stays negative).

questions.prompt: Rewrite using 'enough': "He is so strong that he can lift the stone."
options: He is enough strong to lift the stone.
He is strong enough to lift the stone.
He is strong enough lifting the stone.
He is too strong to lift the stone.
questions.explanation: 'So … that … can' → 'adjective + enough + to-infinitive' ('enough' follows the adjective).
questions.trick: 'enough' comes AFTER an adjective (strong enough) but BEFORE a noun (enough money).

questions.prompt: Begin with 'Hardly': "The match had just started when it began to rain."
options: Hardly the match had started when it began to rain.
Hardly had the match started than it began to rain.
Hardly had the match started when it began to rain.
Hardly did the match start than it began to rain.
questions.explanation: 'Hardly' at the start needs inversion (had the match started) and is followed by 'when'.
questions.trick: No sooner … THAN; Hardly / Scarcely … WHEN — and the auxiliary comes before the subject (inversion).

questions.prompt: In "I know where he lives," the clause 'where he lives' is a/an:
questions.explanation: 'Where he lives' is the object of 'know' (I know what?), so it is a noun clause.
questions.trick: Clause answering 'what?' after the verb → noun clause.

questions.prompt: In "The house where I was born is now a library," the clause 'where I was born' is a/an:
questions.explanation: It describes the noun 'house' (which house?), so it is an adjective clause even though it starts with 'where'.
questions.trick: A clause right after a noun that tells 'which one?' → adjective clause.

questions.prompt: In "Wait here until I return," the clause 'until I return' is a/an:
questions.explanation: 'Until I return' tells how long (time) to wait.

questions.prompt: In "If you heat ice, it melts," the clause 'If you heat ice' is an adverb clause of:
questions.explanation: 'If' introduces a condition.

questions.prompt: In "He was absent because he was ill," the clause 'because he was ill' is an adverb clause of:
questions.explanation: 'Because' gives the reason or cause.

questions.prompt: In "He spoke so softly that nobody heard him," the clause 'that nobody heard him' is an adverb clause of:
questions.explanation: 'So … that' shows the result or consequence of speaking softly.
questions.trick: so … that = result; so that / in order that = purpose.

questions.prompt: In "She works hard so that she may succeed," the clause 'so that she may succeed' is an adverb clause of:
questions.explanation: 'So that … may' shows the aim or purpose.
questions.trick: so … that = result; so that / in order that = purpose.

questions.prompt: Identify the principal (main) clause: "When the bell rang, the students left the classroom."
questions.explanation: The main clause makes sense on its own; 'When the bell rang' is subordinate.

questions.prompt: In "He left the room in a hurry," the words 'in a hurry' form a/an:
questions.explanation: 'In a hurry' tells how he left (modifies the verb) and has no subject-verb, so it is an adverb phrase.
questions.trick: Clause = has its own subject + finite verb; phrase = no subject-verb pair.

questions.prompt: In "He is a man of great wealth," the words 'of great wealth' form a/an:
questions.explanation: It describes the noun 'man' (= a wealthy man) and has no finite verb.
questions.trick: Clause = has its own subject + finite verb; phrase = no subject-verb pair.

questions.prompt: In "To win the match was our only aim," the words 'To win the match' form a/an:
questions.explanation: The infinitive phrase is the subject of 'was', so it does the work of a noun; it has no finite verb, so it is not a clause.

questions.prompt: Replace the phrase 'at sunset' with a clause: "We returned at sunset."
options: We returned which the sun set.
We returned that the sun set.
We returned when the sun set.
questions.explanation: The adverb phrase of time becomes an adverb clause of time introduced by 'when'.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a phrase and NOT a clause?
questions.explanation: 'After the long journey' has no subject and finite verb; the others do.
questions.trick: Clause = has its own subject + finite verb; phrase = no subject-verb pair.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a clause?
questions.explanation: 'As the sun rose' has a subject (the sun) and a finite verb (rose).
questions.trick: Clause = has its own subject + finite verb; phrase = no subject-verb pair.

questions.prompt: In "That he is honest is known to all," the clause 'That he is honest' is a:
questions.explanation: The clause is the subject of 'is known' — it does the work of a noun.

questions.prompt: Identify the adjective clause: "The pen which you gave me is lost."
questions.explanation: 'Which you gave me' describes the noun 'pen'.

questions.prompt: In "I met the girl whose father is a judge," the clause beginning with 'whose' is a/an:
questions.explanation: Introduced by the relative pronoun 'whose', it describes the noun 'girl'.

questions.prompt: How many clauses are there in the sentence: "I knew that he would come when he was free"?
questions.explanation: I knew (main) + that he would come (noun clause) + when he was free (adverb clause) = three finite verbs, three clauses.
questions.trick: Count the finite verbs — one clause per finite verb.

questions.prompt: Identify the noun clause: "Tell me what you want."
questions.explanation: 'What you want' is the direct object of 'tell' and contains a subject and verb.

questions.prompt: In "This is the place where the accident happened," the word 'where' is a:
questions.explanation: 'Where' joins the clause to the noun 'place' and means 'in which' — a relative adverb.

questions.prompt: A clause that can stand alone as a complete sentence is called a/an:
questions.explanation: An independent or main clause expresses a complete thought on its own.

questions.prompt: In "You may sit wherever you like," the clause 'wherever you like' is an adverb clause of:
questions.explanation: 'Wherever' introduces an adverb clause of place.

questions.prompt: In "As he was late, he missed the bus," the clause 'As he was late' is an adverb clause of:
questions.explanation: Here 'as' means 'because' — it gives the reason.

questions.prompt: In "He is taller than his brother is," the clause 'than his brother is' is an adverb clause of:
questions.explanation: 'Than' after a comparative introduces an adverb clause of comparison.

questions.prompt: Identify the noun clause: "She said that she would come early."
questions.explanation: The 'that'-clause is the object of 'said' — a noun clause.
